implementation_notes: Since Java 8 a strategy is normally a functional interface plus a lambda or method reference: the single abstract method is the strategy operation, and java.util.function (Function, UnaryOperator, BinaryOperator, Predicate) plus Comparator are the JDK's ready-made Strategy interfaces. The JDK's own instance of the pattern is Comparator: Collections.sort/List.sort own the sorting workflow and the ordering rule arrives as a strategy, with Comparator.comparing(...).thenComparing(...) composing strategies declaratively. Keep an explicit class (or a static factory method on the interface) when the strategy carries state, documents a business rule, or is reused across modules - a lambda has no useful name in logs or configuration.
pitfalls: A lambda has no identity or readable toString: strategies that appear in logs, metrics or configuration need a named class or an enum constant so the active algorithm is identifiable.
Captured locals must be effectively final, so a strategy that needs mutable state cannot be a lambda; promote it to an object (or an enum with per-constant behaviour).
Comparator is only a strategy while it is a total order: an inconsistent comparator makes List.sort throw 'Comparison method violates its general contract' intermittently, depending on input size.

variants.name: Interface with one class per algorithm (pre-lambda GoF form)
variants.idiom_name: interface PricingStrategy + implementing classes injected into the context
variants.implementation_notes: The original form: an interface declaring the strategy operation, a class per algorithm, and a context holding the interface - still the right shape when the strategy has several operations, carries configuration with invariants, or must be a named type that a DI container resolves and tests mock. It is also the only option on pre-Java-8 runtimes. Because the interface has one abstract method, such a class can additionally be passed as a lambda in modern code, so the two forms interoperate rather than exclude each other.
pitfalls: newing the concrete strategy inside the context (or pulling it from a static holder) hard-wires the algorithm again; inject it or let the DI container supply it.
One class per algorithm multiplies files for trivial rules; a static factory method or an enum constant that returns the lambda keeps small strategies discoverable without a class each.
Interfaces used as strategies drift into god-interfaces: a second abstract method silently breaks lambda compatibility and every existing implementor.
